text: Return an array called answer, where answer at i is the product of all elements except nums at i. It must run in linear time, and without division.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Let me lock in the shape first. Answer at i is the product of everything to the left of i, times everything to the right — that's what except self means. And division is off the table, which is good, because it would break on zeros anyway. Is there a follow-up on space?
Yes — can you do it in constant extra space? The output array doesn't count.

Good — then I can use the output array itself to carry the prefix products, and multiply the suffix in place. Quick check on the example: one, two, three, four gives twenty-four, twelve, eight, six. For index one, that's one times three times four, which is twelve. That matches.

Let me think about avoiding division and the extra space. The brute force multiplies everything else for every index, which is quadratic. This problem reminds me of prefix and suffix products: answer at i is the product of everything left of i, times the product of everything right of i. Two linear sweeps compute both. And if I write the prefixes into the output array first, then fold the suffixes in on a reverse pass, I only need two scalar variables — constant extra space.

Here's the plan. One: start the answer array as all ones. Two: sweep left to right with a running prefix, multiplying it into each cell. Three: sweep right to left with a running suffix, the same way. One thing worth flagging — in each pass I write to the answer before updating the running product. That way the stored value excludes nums at i itself, and the update folds it in for the next index. And it's naturally zero-safe: with no division, a zero only wipes out the positions whose left or right span crosses it, so no special casing. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. Two loops: the forward one multiplies each cell by the running prefix, then folds nums at i into the prefix; the backward one does the same with the suffix. One thing worth flagging — the answer array starts as all ones, so the very first multiply-assign works. If it started at zero, everything would stay zero. And the whole thing reuses the answer array as scratch, so the extra space is just two ints.

Let's dry-run one, two, three, four — expected twenty-four, twelve, eight, six. After the prefix pass, each cell holds its left product: one, one, two, six. The row that matters is index one on the suffix pass: the cell holds one, its left product, and the suffix is twelve, three times four. One times twelve is twelve — exactly the product without the two. Final answer twenty-four, twelve, eight, six. That matches. Corner cases: one, two, zero, four gives zero, zero, eight, zero — only the zero's own index survives. Two zeros give all zeros. A length-two array a, b gives b, a. All check out, with no zero special-casing.

Time is linear — two passes. Extra space is constant — just prefix and suffix; the output array isn't counted, per the follow-up. One more thing — if division were allowed and zeros were guaranteed absent, a single pass dividing the total product by nums at i would be shorter. But it's fragile to zeros, and it's forbidden here. The prefix times suffix structure is robust by construction.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: framing answer at i as left times right, the write-before-update trick that excludes self, and reusing the output array to hit constant extra space — plus noting that it's inherently zero-safe. Good work.
